units.la: AGITVR nunc annus tricesimus quintus, fratres in Christo colendi, quo Esdram & Nehemiam in maiore templo urbis Tigurinae, matutinis horis meis quos habebam auditoribus, exposui. Quo tempore mihi non veniebat in mentem, quod denuo libros illos expositurus, nedum quae in eis notanda observaram, in lucem emissurus essem. Interea mutato consilio, anno superiore, in frequentiore coetu, eos ipsos libros interpretatus, & breui scripto Homilias meas complexus sum, ut aliis quoq; ecclesiarum ministris, qui vel libris necessariis carere coguntur, vel labores illa conquirendi quae debebant, subterfugiunt, nonnihil profuissem: & eos tantum non ad explicationem horum librorum, qui nostris temporibus valde accommodati sunt, invitare: Quia vero nova haec ESDRAE editio, charissimi fratres, in illud ipsum tempus incidit, quo ab amplissimo nostrae urbis Ducentorum Senatu (penes quem summa apud nos est potestas) vnanimi consensu, in reuerendi & clarissimi viri Rodolphi Gualtheri patris & praeceptoris nostri locum, pastor ecclesiae electus sum, vobis hunc librum dedicare uisum est. Gualtherum, ut scitis, curis, uigiliis, laboribus ita exhaustum & confectum, ut pastoris munus amplius obire non posset, amplissimus noster Senatus rude donauit, & ut optime de ecclesia nostra merito, integrum stipendium, quod ante habebat, liberaliter ad obitum usque ei nunerari decreuit: me uero, licet indignum & tanto munere imparem, ne ecclesia nostra pastore careret, illi substituit. Has uero ob causas, uobis fratres colendi, meas illas in ESDRAM Homilias, siue commentarium potius, in uestro nomine apparere uolui, primum ut meum erga uos studium & amorem declararem: deinde ut huius dedicationis occasione, uos, quorum magna apud reliquos ecclesiae ministros est authoritas, in hac persequutione ecclesiae Dei, ad constantiam in puritate doctrinae & vitae integritate, qua ecclesia plurimum aedificatur, exuscitem. Docet enim hic liber ESDRAE, quomodo Deus populum suum post septuaginta annos exilij Babylonici, secundum prædictionem Ieremiae prophetae, Cyri regis permissu, in patriam reduxerit, ut templum rursus extruerent, & politiam collapsam instaurarent. Quomodo item magno & difficili labore, vitae fortunarumq; suarum periculo id fecerint. Vicinae enim gentes, praesides, consiliariis, variis modis, blanditiis, minis, armis, ita eos impediuerunt, diuerunt, ut instauratio templi & urbis Hierosolymorum ad multos annos fuerit dilata. Tandem excitatis a Deo prophetis, qui populum in sancto labore confirmarent, & piis gubernatoribus, qui conatus eorum iuuarent, remotisque omnibus obstaculis, templi ædificium feliciter absolutum fuit. Quid paulo supra nostram memoriam apud nos factum sit, utile erit animo repetere, Huldricus Zuuinglius cum antea Clarona & in Eremo quem vocant diuæ virginis, magna laude docuisset, Tigurum accersitus anno dominicæ natiuitatis 1519. Calendis Ianuarij (quo die anno 1484 natus fuerat) primam concionem apud nos in summo templo habuit, postero die qui dominicus erat, Euangelium Matthæi profugesto publicè enarrare cæpit, & patres nostros ex captiuitate Babylonica paulatim educere, templum q; domini spirituale instaurare, ab aliis quoq; suæ ordinis hominibus amplissimo Senatu Tigurino non parum adiutus. Quæ vero nascenti ecclesiæ impedimenta per falsos fratres, hypocritas & tyrannos obiecta sint, longum esset commemorare. Nostro tempore Satan vehementius graßatur, totumq; quasi orbem ad arma concitat, & fratres quoq; nostros aduersus nos instigat, ut omnes ecclesias funditus euertere, arcem superstitionis recuperare, suamq; tyrannidem stabilire possit. Ingentia vero illa pericula, quæ nos undiq; circumstant, nequaquam a vera religionis professione nos abstrerre debent, sed potius excitare, ut exemplo populi Dei qui e capti uita te redierat, quo plures obices Satan ad impediendum euangelij liberum cursum ingerit, eo magis nos ad studium aedificandae ecclesiae accendamur. Neq; dubitandum est, quin si nostrum officium sedulo fecerimus docendo, sanctè viuendo, precando: neq; solùm alios ecclesiae ministros collegas nostros, sed et plebe nostrae curae commissam, ad veram poenitentiam excitauerimus, Deus gratiam et spiritum suum largiturus sit, quò templi aedificium inuito Antichristo magis magisq; progrediatur. Solet enim Deus suos fideles rebus afflictissimis & desperatissimis, mirabiliter contra hominum opinionem iuuare, conseruare, hostiumq; ecclesiae certam iam sibi victoriam promittentium spem & conatus frustrari. Quae omnia in hoc libro, tanquam in speculo ad nostram doctrinam & consolationem proponuntur. Sed quid noctuas Athenas? Vos etiam atq; etiam rogo, fratres, ut literarium hoc munusculum, quod animo syncero & candido vobis offero (animus in muneribus optimus esse vulgo dicitur) candidè à me accipiatis & perlegatis. Faxit Deus optimus Max, ut omnium nostrum ministerium, ecclesiae ipsius fructuosum sit & salutare. Valete in Christo charissimi fratres, & in vestro munere estote sedulì. Tigurì mense februario anno Dominicae natiuitatis 1586.
units.tr: It is now the thirty-fifth year, brothers in Christ to be honoured, since I expounded Ezra and Nehemiah in the great church of the city of Zurich, in the morning hours, to the hearers I then had. At that time it did not occur to me that I would expound those books again, still less that I would publish the things I had noted in them. Since then, however, I changed my plan. Last year, before a fuller assembly, I interpreted those same books and gathered my Homilies into a brief written form, so that I might be of some help also to other ministers of the churches, who are either forced to go without the necessary books or shrink from the labour of seeking out what they ought to have. I invited them, as it were, to an explanation of these books, which are very well suited to our times. But since this new edition of Ezra, beloved brothers, has fallen at the very time when I was chosen by the unanimous vote of our most distinguished Senate of Two Hundred (in whose hands the highest power among us lies) to succeed the reverend and most distinguished man Rudolf Gwalther, our father and teacher, I thought it fitting to dedicate this book to you. As you know, Gwalther was so worn out and exhausted by cares, vigils and labours that he could no longer discharge the duties of a minister. Our most distinguished Senate granted him his release, and, having deserved so well of our church, it generously decided to pay him his full former stipend until his death. As for me, although I am unworthy and unequal to so great an office, it appointed me as his substitute, so that our church would not be without a minister. For these reasons, brothers to be honoured, I wished that my Homilies on EZRA, or rather commentary, should appear under your name: first, to declare my zeal and love towards you; then, that on the occasion of this dedication I might rouse you, whose authority among the other ministers of the church is great, to constancy in the purity of doctrine and integrity of life, by which the church is chiefly built up, in this persecution of the church of God. For this book of Ezra teaches how God, after seventy years of the Babylonian exile, according to the prediction of the prophet Jeremiah, by the permission of King Cyrus, led his people back into their homeland, so that they might rebuild the temple and restore their fallen polity. It also teaches with what great and difficult labour, and at the risk of their lives and fortunes, they did so. For the neighbouring peoples, their governors and counsellors, hindered them in various ways, by flattery, threats and arms, so that the restoration of the temple and of the city of Jerusalem was delayed for many years. At last, prophets were raised up by God to strengthen the people in their holy labour, and pious governors to support their efforts; all obstacles were removed, and the building of the temple was happily completed. It will be useful to recall in our own minds what happened among us a little before our own memory. Huldrych Zwingli, after he had taught at Glarus and in the hermitage called of the blessed Virgin with great praise, was summoned to Zurich in the year of the Lord's birth 1519, on the first day of January (the day on which he had been born in 1484). He preached his first sermon among us in the great church, and on the following day, which was a Sunday, he began to expound publicly the Gospel of Matthew, and gradually to lead our fathers out of the Babylonian captivity and to restore the spiritual temple of the Lord, being not a little helped also by other men of his order, and by the most distinguished Senate of Zurich. As to the hindrances that were raised against the infant church by false brethren, hypocrites and tyrants, it would be long to recount them. In our own time Satan rages more violently, rouses almost the whole world to arms, and stirs up our brothers also against us, so that he may overthrow all churches to the foundations, recover the citadel of superstition and establish his tyranny. Yet those great dangers which surround us on every side ought by no means to drive us away from the profession of true religion, but rather to stir us up, so that, by the example of the people of God who had returned from captivity, the more obstacles Satan puts in the way of the free course of the gospel, the more we may be kindled to the zeal of building up the church. Nor is there any doubt that if we faithfully do our duty by teaching, living holily and praying, and by rousing to true repentance not only the other ministers, our colleagues, but also the people committed to our care, God will grant his grace and his Spirit, so that the building of the temple may advance more and more, Antichrist being unwilling. For God is wont to help his faithful in the most afflicted and desperate circumstances, wonderfully, against human expectation, to preserve them, and to frustrate the hopes and attempts of the enemies of the church, who already promise themselves certain victory. All these things are set forth in this book, as in a mirror, for our teaching and consolation. But why carry owls to Athens? I beg you again and again, brothers, to receive from me and read through this little literary gift, which I offer you with a sincere and open heart (it is commonly said that the heart is the best gift). May God, the best and greatest, grant that the ministry of all of us may be fruitful and salutary to his church itself. Farewell in Christ, most beloved brothers, and be diligent in your office. At Zurich, in the month of February, in the year of the Lord's birth 1586.

LVDOVICI LAVATERI TIGVRINAE ECCLESIAE MINISTRI, IN PRIMVM Librum Efdrae, Homiliae. HOMILIA I. De authore, argumento, vsu & eloquutione huius Libri.
units.tr: Homilies on the First Book of Ezra by Ludwig Lavater, Minister of the Church of Zurich. HOMILY I. On the author, subject, use and style of this Book.

units.la: EZDRAS ex tribu Leui sacerdos fuit, Saraiae summi Pontificis filius, quem Nabuchodonosor vnà cum alijs primarijs viris, in Riblath, quae alio nomine Antiochia vocatur, capite plecti iussit, eò quòd cum Zedechia Iudaeorum rege contra ipsum conspirauerant. Frater Ezdrae, Iosedek pontifex fuit, & cum eo in Babylonem abductus est. Genealogia Ezdrae contexitur infra 7. capite vbi appellatur scriba, & promptus atq; expeditus scriba, in lege Dei. Hebraei per scribas aliquando notarios intelligunt, plerunque verò doctos. Eorum enim officium fuit, scripturas intelligere & interpretari. Quomodo Ezdras scripturas tractarit, postea capite 7. verf. 6. audiemus. De scribis Matth. 2. legimus, quòd statim responderint Herodi ex propheta Michea, vbi Christus nascitur esset. Hic Ezdras reuersus in patriam, magno zelo vsus est. De peritia rerum diuinarum qua praeditus fuit, & animi integritate, primus hic liber italoquitur: Ezdras parauit cor suum, vt inuestigaret Legem Domini: & faceret & doceret in Israel, praeceptum & iudicum. In Suidae collectaneis, appellatur νομομαθὴς ἀρίστος, hoc est, optimus interpres & doctor legum. Iosephus testatur Ezdram mortuum in aetate grandi, & Hierosoli mis honorifice sepultum. Qui plura de Ezdra volunt cognoscere, legant Theodori Bibliandri professoris Theologiae in schola Tigurina explicationem Somnij Ezdrae, quae publicè extat. Scripsit hunc librum, in quo res praecipuas, quas ipse gessit complectitur, vt Iosue, vt Samuel & alij. Ascribunt ei etiam secundum librum, qui tamen est Nehemiae. D. Hieronymus testatur apud Hebraeos Efdrae Nehemiaeq; sermones, in vnum volumé coarctatos.
units.tr: Ezra was a priest of the tribe of Levi, the son of Seraiah the high priest, whom Nebuchadnezzar ordered to be beheaded at Riblah, which is also called Antioch, together with other leading men, because they had conspired against him with Zedekiah, king of the Jews. Ezra's brother Jeshua was high priest, and was carried off with him to Babylon. Ezra's genealogy is given in chapter 7, where he is called a scribe, and a ready and skilled scribe in the law of God. The Hebrews sometimes understand "scribes" to mean notaries, but mostly learned men. Their office was to understand and interpret the Scriptures. How Ezra handled the Scriptures we shall hear later, in chapter 7, verse 6. In Matthew 2 we read that the scribes immediately answered Herod from the prophet Micah where Christ was to be born. Ezra, returning to his homeland, showed great zeal. This first book itself speaks of the skill in divine matters with which he was endowed, and of his integrity of mind: "Ezra had prepared his heart to seek the law of the Lord, and to do it and to teach in Israel statute and judgment" (Ezra 7:10). In the collection of Suidas he is called νομομαθὴς ἄριστος [nomomathēs aristos], that is, the best interpreter and teacher of the laws. Josephus bears witness that Ezra died at a great age and was buried with honour in Jerusalem. Those who wish to learn more about Ezra should read the explanation of Ezra's Vision by Theodor Bibliander, professor of theology in the school of Zurich, which is published. Ezra wrote this book, in which he records the principal events in which he himself took part, as Joshua and Samuel and others did. They also ascribe to him the second book, which is however Nehemiah's. St Jerome testifies that among the Hebrews the sermons of Ezra and Nehemiah were gathered into one volume.

units.la: A stari. Apud Latinos & Græcos distinćti sunt libri. Tertius & quartus,quos vulgò Ezdræ tribuunt,non sunt in Canone diui-norum librorum : quanquam multa lestu non indigna conti-neant,præsertim quartus. Veteres Hebræi tribuunt etiam Ez-dræ,Malachiæ sermonem propheticum, quod D. Hieronymus quoque sequitur,eò quòd tempus & titulus conueniant. Mala-chias enim significat nuncium vel legatnm Dei, quod munus Ezdras præclarè gessit.Deinde res easdem tractat,quas historia Ezdræ. Creditur etiam author librorum Paralipomenon.Nam exordium libri Ezdræ coincidit cum fine secundi Paralipome-non.Refertur adhæc Psalmos in hunc quo nunc leguntur ordi-nem,disposuisse.Quin vniuersas scripturas sacras,Ezdræ memo-ria,cum incendio absumtæ essent,restitutas dicūt. Tertullianus vetustissimus scriptor,de prophetia Enoch differes:potuit abo-lefactam Noe in spiritu reformare: quemadmodum & Hierofo-lymis Babylonica expugnatione deletis, omne instrumentum Iudaicæ literaturæ per Ezdram constat restauratum. Et Suidas in nomine Ezdras: ὃς τὴν μὲν εὑρεῖν τῶν βιβλίων τὰς γραφὰς ἀναμνημονέσας, παρέδωκε τοῖς τὸ ἔθνους, hoc est,qui repetens memoria scripturas librorum, qui non sunt inuenti, populari-bus suis tradidit. Eusebius quoq; hanc traditionem amplexus est. Hoc autem nō videtur intelligendum de authenticis libris prophetarum,sed potius de expositionibus quibusdam,quæ in bibliothecis repositæ,perierint vrbe inflamata.Quis enim cre-det Iechoniam regem, & qui cum eo sponte in exilium abierût, suadente Ieremia,diuinos libros vnicum exilij solamen,non se-cum tulisse? Danielem constat in captiuitate librum Ieremiæ le-gisse. Cumq; Deus vasa sacra,in tam horrendis confusionibus, omnia conseruarit, quis existimaret diuinos illos libros,non e-tiam fuisse ab eo conseruatos? Si res aliter haberet, non Moses, non Isaias,sed pro omnibus Ezdras legeretur.
units.tr: Among the Latins and Greeks the books are distinguished. The third and fourth books, which are commonly attributed to Ezra, are not in the canon of the divine books, although they contain many things worth reading, especially the fourth. The ancient Hebrews also attribute to Ezra the prophetic oracle of Malachi, which St Jerome also follows, because the time and the title agree. For Malachi means "messenger" or "envoy" of God, which office Ezra performed admirably. Next, the book treats the same matters as the history of Ezra. He is also believed to be the author of the books of Chronicles, for the beginning of the book of Ezra coincides with the end of the second book of Chronicles. It is further reported that he arranged the Psalms in the order in which they are now read. Indeed, they say that all the sacred Scriptures were restored by Ezra's memory, after they had been consumed by fire. Tertullian, a very ancient writer, in his treatise on the prophecy of Enoch, says that Noah could have reformed by the Spirit what had been destroyed; and likewise, when Jerusalem had been destroyed by the Babylonian conquest, it is established that every record of Jewish literature was restored through Ezra. And Suidas, under the name Ezra, says: "who, recalling by memory the writings of the books, handed them down to his people" [ὃς τὴν μὲν εὑρεῖν τῶν βιβλίων τὰς γραφὰς ἀναμνημονεύσας, παρέδωκε τοῖς ἰδίοις τοῦ ἔθνους]. Eusebius also embraced this tradition. But this is not to be understood of the authentic books of the prophets, but rather of certain expositions which, having been stored in libraries, perished when the city was set on fire. For who would believe that King Jeconiah, and those who went into exile with him of their own accord, at the urging of Jeremiah, did not carry with them the divine books, the sole consolation of the exile? It is established that Daniel read the book of Jeremiah during the captivity. And since God preserved the sacred vessels amid such horrible confusion, who would suppose that those divine books were not also preserved by him? If the matter stood otherwise, it would not be Moses or Isaiah, but Ezra, who would be read in place of all.

units.la: Scopus & argumentum huius libri est,quomodo Deus po-pulum suum ex captiuitate Babylonica reduxerit. Quod vt me-lius intelligatur,paulò altius ex fine librorum Regum & Parali-pomenon repetemus,quando,quomodo,quare,per quos capti-ui abducti sint. Regnum decem tribuum,post varias clades,tan-dem euersum & deletum fuit. Phul & Teglatphulassar maximâ decem tribuum partem armis ceperunt.2.Reg 15.1.Paral.5.Po-stea Salmanasar rex Assyriorum, capta Samaria, & occiso rege Oseæ,qui vltimus fuit in hoc regno, maximam populi partem in Mediam,Persiam & alias regiones dispersit,& alias incolas in hoc regnum traduxit. Causæ interitus huius regni fusè commorantur 2.Reg.17.cap.& in prophetarum concionibus. Præcipuæ fuerunt,idololatria, contemtus verbi diuini,omnis generis scelera,&c. Durauit hoc regnum, fecundum Theodori Bibliandri calculum,annis 263.
units.tr: The aim and subject of this book is how God led his people back from the Babylonian captivity. To understand this better, we shall go back somewhat further, to the end of the books of Kings and Chronicles, when, how, why, and by whom they were carried off into captivity. The kingdom of the ten tribes, after various disasters, was at last overthrown and destroyed. Pul and Tiglath-pileser took the greater part of the ten tribes by force of arms (2 Kings 15; 1 Chronicles 5). Afterwards Shalmaneser, king of the Assyrians, took Samaria, and when King Hoshea, who was the last in this kingdom, had been killed, he scattered the greater part of the people into Media, Persia and other regions, and brought other inhabitants into this kingdom. The causes of the destruction of this kingdom are set out at length in 2 Kings 17 and in the sermons of the prophets. The chief were idolatry, contempt of the divine word, and every kind of wickedness. According to the calculation of Theodor Bibliander, this kingdom lasted 263 years.

units.la: Deleto illo regno,prophetæ regni Iudæ hominibus comi-nati sunt,quod & ipsi,nisi vicinorum & fratrum suorum exemplo cautiores fierent,abducendi essent in captiuitatem:sed surdis ceciderunt fabulam. Itaq; post Iofiæ regis optimi obitū,res omnes ad interitum ruebant.Ioachas eius filius quem populus regè creauerat, Ægyptius rex reuersus ex bello Assyriaco, quo vicerat Nabuchodonosorem Priscum, in Ægyptum abduxit,& fratrem eius Ioachimum regem costituit. Postea cum Nabu-chodonosor Magnus instaurato bello, vltus esset patrem,deui-ćto regeÆgypti,ipse Ioachimum sibi tributarium fecit.qui post tres annos cum recusaret tributū, à Nabuchodonosore fuit in Babylonem abductus, & multi cum eo, Daniel & socij eius,E-zechiel & alij. Filium eius Ioachim qui & Iechonias dicitur,patris loco regem constituit, qui postea cum Nabuchodonosore misso exercitu Hierosolyma obsidione cinxisset, suasu Ieremiæ deditione facta, sponte cum suis in Babylonem migrauit. Nabu-chodonosor regem creauit Zedechiam,qui cum ad Ægyptium defecisset,& illum Babylonius tandem in captiuitatem traxit.
units.tr: When that kingdom had been destroyed, the prophets threatened the men of the kingdom of Judah that they too would be carried into captivity unless they became more careful by the example of their neighbours and brothers; but they fell upon deaf ears. Thus, after the death of the best king, Josiah, all things rushed to ruin. His son Jehoahaz, whom the people had made king, was carried off into Egypt by the Egyptian king, who was returning from the war with Assyria in which he had defeated Nebuchadnezzar the Elder, and he set up his brother Jehoiakim as king. Afterwards, when Nebuchadnezzar the Great renewed the war to avenge his father, and had subdued the king of Egypt, he made Jehoiakim his tributary; and after three years, when Jehoiakim refused to pay tribute, he was carried off by Nebuchadnezzar to Babylon, and with him many others: Daniel and his companions, Ezekiel and others. He set up Jehoiakim's son Jehoiachin, who is also called Jeconiah, as king in his father's place. Afterwards, when Jeconiah had besieged Jerusalem with an army sent by Nebuchadnezzar, a surrender was made at the urging of Jeremiah, and he went voluntarily with his people into Babylon. Nebuchadnezzar made Zedekiah king; when Zedekiah revolted to the Egyptian, the Babylonian at last dragged him into captivity.

units.la: Atq; ita Iudæi regnum, vrbes templum & libertatem suam amiserunt,& in longinquam terrá abductì sunt,in qua perman-serunt 70. annis, qui ab vltimo anno Ioachimi,vel à migratione Iechoniæ quæ paulò post facta est,numerantur.
units.tr: And so the Jews lost their kingdom, their cities, their temple and their freedom, and they were carried off into a distant land, in which they remained seventy years, which are counted from the last year of Jehoiakim, or from the migration of Jeconiah, which took place shortly afterwards.

units.la: Interea Babylonij insolenter vićtoria vsi sunt,cōtumelia assi-cientes ipsum Deum. In Psal. 137. Postulant à mœstis Iudæis,vt ludant cytharis,& de sua religione canant,&c.Cogebātur Iudæi quotidie multa indigna audire& aspicere toto tempore exilij, omniū ludibrijs & iniurijs expositi. Excitauit igitur Deus Me-dos & Persas,qui vrbem Babylonem euerterent, sicut per suos seruos prophetas Ifa.13.14.& Ierem.50.51. prædixerat.
units.tr: Meanwhile the Babylonians made insolent use of their victory, heaping insults even upon God himself (Psalm 137). They demanded of the sorrowing Jews that they play on their harps and sing of their religion, and so on. The Jews were compelled every day, throughout the whole time of the exile, to hear and see many shameful things, being exposed to the mockery and injuries of all. God therefore stirred up the Medes and Persians to overthrow the city of Babylon, as he had foretold through his servant prophets (Isaiah 13 and 14; Jeremiah 50 and 51).

units.la: Cæterum Deus Iudæis promiserat,quòd per Cyrū liberandi essent,scribit itaq; in hoc libro Ezdras,quomodo Cyrus Iudæis copiá fecerit redeundi in patriam, & ædificandi templū,& quo modo paulatim alij post alios in patriam redierint.Primū Zoro-babel qui ex regio sanguine fuit,Iefua pōtifex & alij, iter ingres-si,ac in patriam reuersi,extruxerunt altare, fundamentū templi locarunt:adiunxerunt se Samaritani, vt ædificium impedirent, quòd & fecerunt,cū Cyrus bellis occupatus esset,Cábyse patris vices gerente vfq; ad fecundum Darij annum. Sub Dario hor-tatu prophetarum redeunt Iudæi ad opus templi iam diu inter missum,præfecti regij fe opponunt,sed non vehementer,fcribút ad regem, qui mandat illis ne ædificantes impediant. Septimo anno Darij, Ezdras cum regio diplomate venit, iudices constituit,& peccata procerum correxit.Vicesimo anno venit Nehemias,qui vrbem instaurauit & muniuit:populum vsuris & exa-ctionibus leuauit.
units.tr: Moreover, God had promised the Jews that they would be set free through Cyrus. So Ezra writes in this book how Cyrus gave the Jews the means to return to their homeland and to build the temple, and how, little by little, one after another, they returned to their homeland. First Zerubbabel, who was of royal blood, Jeshua the high priest and others, having set out on the journey and returned to their homeland, erected an altar and laid the foundation of the temple. The Samaritans joined them, in order to hinder the building, which they did, while Cyrus was occupied with wars, his son Cambyses acting as his deputy, until the second year of Darius. Under Darius, at the urging of the prophets, the Jews returned to the work on the temple, which had long been interrupted; the royal officials opposed them, but not vehemently; they wrote to the king, who ordered them not to hinder the builders. In the seventh year of Darius, Ezra came with a royal decree, appointed judges, and corrected the sins of the nobles. In the twentieth year Nehemiah came, who restored and fortified the city and relieved the people of usury and exactions.

units.la: Continet hæc historia annos circiter 70. tot enim à primo anno Cyri vfq; ad 32. annum Darij, quo muri absoluti sunt, numerantur.
units.tr: This history covers about seventy years, for that is the time from the first year of Cyrus to the thirty-second year of Darius, when the walls were completed.

units.la: Partes huius libri sunt duæ.In priore parte, quæ 6. capita habet, ostenditur copiose, quomodo Zerubabel & Iesus primū cum parte populi ascenderint. In altera parte,quæ 4.posteriori bus capitibus absoluitur, continetur fecundus ascensus populi ex Babylone Ezdra duce,sub Artaxerxis anno 7.
units.tr: This book has two parts. In the first part, which has six chapters, it is shown at length how Zerubbabel and Jeshua first went up with a part of the people. The second part, which is completed in the last four chapters, contains the second going up of the people from Babylon under Ezra as leader, in the seventh year of Artaxerxes.

units.la: Vt autem aliorum sacrorum librorum immensa est vtilitas, ita huius quoq; libri.Ex eo enim videmus veritatem & certitudinem verbi Dei in promissis,minis, vaticinijs. Res erat incredibilis Babylonem quæ caput erat orbis, & regia sedes summi imperij, aliquando capiendam esse & euertendam,ac populum hunc liberandum ex illa tyrannide, sed cum tempus fatale appe teret,Deus nullo negotio id perfecit.Prophetę in prædictionibus rerum futurarum,verbis præteriti temporis vtûtur, vt tam certò euenturas credamus,ac fi iam euenissent.
units.tr: As the benefit of the other sacred books is immense, so too is the benefit of this one. For from it we see the truth and certainty of the word of God in its promises, threats and prophecies. It seemed incredible that Babylon, which was the head of the world and the royal seat of supreme power, would one day be taken and overthrown, and that this people would be freed from that tyranny. But when the fated time drew near, God accomplished it without any difficulty. The prophets, in predicting future events, use the verbs of past time, so that we may believe they will come to pass as surely as if they had already come to pass.

units.la: Deinde quàm ægrè procedat ædificiū ecclesiæ,ex hoc libro apparet.Diu res est protracta.Hodie quoq; fi ædificandæ sint ædes sacræ,aut instaurandæ, vix adduci possunt homines vt hoc faciant:at fi idolis aliquid construendum fit, res non diu differtur.Spiritualis quoq; templi ædificium,non nisi summo labore procedit.
units.tr: Next, how slowly the building of the Church advances is apparent from this book. The matter was delayed for a long time. Even today, if sacred buildings are to be erected or restored, men can scarcely be brought to do it; but if something is to be built for idols, the matter is not put off for long. The building of the spiritual temple too proceeds only with the greatest labour.

units.la: Colligimus præterea, quibus artibus Antichristus & eius fa tellites ædificium ecclesiæ impediant.
units.tr: We also gather from this the arts by which Antichrist and his satellites hinder the building of the Church.

units.la: Item,quanta vigilantia & prudentia opus fit,ne ab hostibus ecclesiæ circumueniamur.Multa etiam alia,quæ suis locis explicabuntur,ex hoc libro hauriemus. Hæc liberatio populi ab exilio Babylonico,& reditus in patriam,sicut & edućtio ex Ægypto, typus fuit redemtionis qua per Chriftũ colligendi erat ipsi & alij fideles ex vniuerso orbe ad vnitatē fidei & corpus ecclesiæ, ad regnum Dei,& liberandi à tyrānide diaboli,damnatione æterna,& donandi vita æterna, ac reducendi in veram patriam.
units.tr: Likewise, how great watchfulness and prudence is needed, so that we are not surrounded by the enemies of the Church. We shall also draw many other things from this book, which will be explained in their places. This liberation of the people from the Babylonian exile, and their return to their homeland, was, just as the leading out from Egypt was, a type of the redemption by which Christ was to gather to himself, from the whole world, both himself and the other faithful, into the unity of faith and the body of the Church, into the kingdom of God; and to free them from the tyranny of the devil and from eternal damnation, to grant them eternal life, and to lead them back into their true homeland.

units.la: Eloquutio huius libri, partim est Hebraica, partim Syriaca. Cæterum vt hunc librum,maximi nostris præsertim temporibus momenti,nobis familiarem reddamus, diligenter primum domi historia cognoscenda erit, & feries eius animo imprimenda. Deus bone quoties legimus inanes fabulas, cur non sacra potius tractamus?Si quæ occurrunt quę difficultatem habent, postea inter interpretandum omnia percipiemus melius.
units.tr: The language of this book is partly Hebrew and partly Syriac. Moreover, so that we may make this book, which is of the greatest importance especially in our times, familiar to us, the history must first be learned carefully at home, and its sequence impressed on the mind. Good God, how often do we read empty fables, why do we not rather take up sacred things? If there are passages that present difficulty, we shall understand everything better afterwards, while interpreting.

units.la: CAPVT I.
units.tr: CHAPTER I.

units.la: HOMILIA II.
units.tr: HOMILY II.

units.la: Deus cor Cyri mouit, vt facultatem daret Israelitis proficiscendi in patriam.
units.tr: God moved the heart of Cyrus so that he gave the Israelites the opportunity to go back to their homeland.

units.la: Anno primo Chores Regis Paras, vt perficeretur Verbum Iehouæ ex ore Irmeiah, excitauit Iehouah spiritum Chores Regis Paras, qui edictum pro mulgauit per vniuersum regnum suum, & etiam scripto, dicendo.
units.tr: In the first year of Cyrus king of Persia, that the word of Jehovah spoken by the mouth of Jeremiah might be fulfilled, Jehovah stirred up the spirit of Cyrus king of Persia, who issued a proclamation throughout all his kingdom, and also in writing, saying.

units.la: PRIMVM caput in tres partes potest distingui. In prima, Cyrus voce & scripto concedit Iudæis, vt in patriam redeant, suisq; mandat, vt eis sint auxilio. In secunda, primores Iudæorum viam ingressi dicuntur, adiuti à subiectis Cyri. In tertia rex Cyrus aurea & argentea vasa, quæ Nabuchodonosor ex templo acceperat, Iudæis Hierosolymam abeuntibus reddi iubet.
units.tr: The first chapter can be divided into three parts. In the first, Cyrus, by word and by writing, grants the Jews permission to return to their homeland, and orders his subjects to help them. In the second, the leading men of the Jews are said to have set out on the journey, assisted by Cyrus's subjects. In the third, King Cyrus orders that the golden and silver vessels which Nebuchadnezzar had taken from the temple be given back to the Jews as they leave for Jerusalem.

units.la: Quoad primam partem, Deus Cyri regis spiritum excitasse dicitur, hoc est mentem commouisse, vt præcones in regnis suis, item edicto passim proposito, Iudæis veniam daret redeundi in patriam. Tempus annotatur anno primo Cyri regis Persarum. Non primo anno particularium regnorum, sed monarchiæ. Cum ipse & Darius rex Medorum eius auunculus, euertissent monarchiam Chaldæorum, & eorum metropolin Babylonem cepissent, Darius tenuit monarchiam biennio, quo mortuo, Cyrus hæreditario iure monarcha effectus, Iudæis potestatem redeundi in patriam concesit.
units.tr: As to the first part, God is said to have stirred up the spirit of King Cyrus, that is, to have moved his mind, so that heralds throughout his kingdoms, and likewise by a proclamation posted everywhere, would grant the Jews leave to return to their homeland. The time is noted as the first year of Cyrus king of the Persians: not the first year of the particular kingdoms, but of the monarchy. When he and Darius king of the Medes, his uncle, had overthrown the monarchy of the Chaldeans and taken their metropolis, Babylon, Darius held the monarchy for two years. On his death, Cyrus became monarch by hereditary right and granted the Jews the power to return to their homeland.

units.la: Adducitur testimonium Ieremiæ, capite 25. Ostendit prophetam, quot annis frustra illos ad pœnitentiam hortatus sit, abducendos igitur à Nabuchodonosore, cui seruituri sint 70. annis. Quod postea factum est. Anno enim vltimo Ioachimi regis multi abducti sunt, & cum eius filio Iechonia, qui eodem anno abductus est, prophetæ suasu, sponte se dedens regi. Capite 29, mittit Propheta epistolam ad captiuos, initio regni Zedechiæ, qua eos hortatur, ne falsis prophetis credant, qui turbabant eos dicentes, Non diu duraturam hanc captiuitatem, &c. nam post 70. demum annos reducendos: nec esse quod antea sperent liberationem. Isaias consolationem scripsit eorum qui in Babylonem ducendi erant, quæ à capite 40. vsque ad 49. extenditur. Inter alia illos hoc argumento consolatur, quod reducendi aliquando sint, edens nomen Cyri, per quem Deus Babylonem capi, & populum liberari velit, circiter 140. annis, antequam ille nasceretur. Iosephus scribit libro Antiquitatum 11. Capite primo, Cyro regi oblatum esse volumen Isaiæ à Iudæis, quo lecto miratum esse vatis diuinitatem, atque incensum cupiditate ea exequendi, quæ de se scripta inuenerat. Si cum Cyro rege Pharaonem conferas, videbis insignem illius pietatem, statim enim Deo obsequitur, hic nullis prodigijs, nullis adhortationibus seruorum Dei Moysis & Aaronis, adduci potuit, vt Deo obsequeretur. Edictum regis mox sequitur.
units.tr: The testimony of Jeremiah, chapter 25, is adduced. It shows how many years the prophet had urged them in vain to repentance, and that they were therefore to be carried away by Nebuchadnezzar, whom they would serve for seventy years. This was afterwards fulfilled. In the last year of King Jehoiakim many were carried away, together with his son Jeconiah, who was taken away in the same year, having surrendered himself to the king of his own accord on the prophet's advice. In chapter 29 the Prophet sends a letter to the captives at the beginning of the reign of Zedekiah, in which he exhorts them not to believe the false prophets who were troubling them by saying that this captivity would not last long, etc. For they would be brought back only after seventy years, and they should not hope for deliverance before then. Isaiah wrote a consolation for those who were to be led into Babylon, which extends from chapter 40 to chapter 49. Among other things he comforts them with the argument that they would at some time be brought back, naming Cyrus, through whom God wished Babylon to be taken and the people set free, about 140 years before he was born. Josephus writes in book 11 of the Antiquities, chapter 1, that the volume of Isaiah was offered to King Cyrus by the Jews, and that when he read it he was amazed at the divinity of the prophet and was inflamed with desire to carry out the things which he found written about himself. If you compare King Cyrus with Pharaoh, you will see his remarkable piety: for Cyrus at once obeyed God, whereas Pharaoh could not be brought to obey God by any miracles or any exhortations of the servants of God, Moses and Aaron. The king's edict soon follows.

units.la: Videamus nunc quæ nobis ex initio huius libri discenda sint.
units.tr: Let us now see what we are to learn from the beginning of this book.

units.la: 1. Elicimus quo loco habenda sint vaticinia & scripta Ieremiæ in vniuersum. Dicit scriptura, verbum Domini prolatum esse per os Ieremiæ. Idem iudicandum de alijs quoq; propheticis item de apostolicis sermonibus & libris. Ieremias non potuisset dicere, an hoc vel illo anno reuersuri essent, imo quid postero die futurum esset, nisi Deus illi reuelasset. Ita alij quoq;. Zacharias pater Ioannis Baptistæ Lucæ 1. capite, in suo cantico: Deus, inquit loquutus est per os suorum sanctorum prophetarum. D. Petrus Actorum 3. capite bis dicit, Deum loquutum esse per os suorum prophetarum. Capite 4. loquutum esse dicit, per os Dauidis serui sui. Ideo sæpe præmittunt exordiolum illud suis concionibus: Verbum Domini factum est ad me: sic dixit Dominus. Matthæi 10. Vos non estis qui loquimini, sed spiritus patris vestri qui loquitur in vobis. D. Paulus laudat Thessalonicenses suos in priore epistola, quod verba sua non audiuerint, vt verba hominis: sed sicut reuera erat, vt verbum Dei. Differunt in hoc sacræ literæ ab alijs scriptis, siue patrum siue aliorum, quod sunt amusis & regula, item Lydius lapis ad quem alia omnia exigere & examinare oportet. Multi sacras literas contemnunt, ideo non mirum, si quiduis facere parati sint, & in aerumnis positi, nullam consolation habeant.
units.tr: 1. We learn in what place the prophecies and writings of Jeremiah are to be held in general. Scripture says that the word of the Lord was spoken through the mouth of Jeremiah. The same judgement is to be made of the other prophetic and likewise of the apostolic sermons and books. Jeremiah could not have said whether they would return this year or that, or indeed what would happen the next day, unless God had revealed it to him. So too with others. Zechariah, the father of John the Baptist, in his canticle in Luke chapter 1 says: God, he says, has spoken by the mouth of his holy prophets. Acts 3 says twice that God spoke by the mouth of his prophets. Chapter 4 says that he spoke by the mouth of David his servant. Hence they often prefix that little introduction to their sermons: "The word of the Lord came to me: thus says the Lord." Matthew 10: "It is not you who speak, but the Spirit of your Father who speaks in you." St Paul praises his Thessalonians in his first epistle, because they did not hear his words as the words of man, but, as they truly were, as the word of God. In this the sacred letters differ from other writings, whether of the Fathers or of others, because they are the rule and norm, and like the Lydian stone, to which all other things must be brought and tested. Many despise the sacred letters, and so it is no wonder if they are ready to do anything whatever, and, when they are in distress, have no consolation.

units.la: 2. Exemplum habemus illius sententiae Prouerbiorum 21. Ve-lut riui aquarum, cor regis in manu Domini, ad omne quod vult inclinat illud. Haec sententia non tantum de regibus, sed etiam de priuatis accipienda est, quorum corda etiam flectit quocunq; voluerit, vt id faciant, quod alioqui minime facturi essent. Cyrus noluisset carere opera Iudaeorum, sed Deus efficit, vt eos manumittat. Habemus in hoc libro huius rei etiam alia exempla. In hoc capite de populo, cuius spiritum Deus dicitur suscitasse 5. capite. Tithnai & socij se humanos Iudaeis praebuerunt, & tantum non apud regem pro illis intercedunt. Capite 6. de Dario quod decretum Cyri quesiuerit, & praeceperit suis, ne impedirent aedificantes, &c. Aliud exemplum afferam ex Iosepho de Alexandro magno, qui Persarum monarchiam, quam hic Cyrus extruxerat, tandem euertit. Is cum exercitu contra Iudaeos Hierosolymam mouit, quibus infestus erat, quod in ob fidionem Cyri opem petenti non tulerant, idq; propter beneficia quae a regibus Persicis acceperant. Iaddus summus pontifex ornatus sua velte, & sacerdotes, seniores item, effusi sunt illi obuiam, vt pacem supplices peterent. Alexander viso summo pontifice, de equo descendit eumque salutauit. Ducibus interrogantibus, cur ita se demitteret? respondit, in Macedonia talem speciem ei in somnis obuersatam esse, iusfiteq; vt bellum Persis inferret: seq; adiutum a Deo, cuius ille seruus esset, & primo libro Paralipomenon quinto capite, Deus etiam dicitur suscitasse spiritum Phul regis Assur, & spiritum Tiglathpilnefer regis Afsur, vt Rubenitas, Gaditas, & dimidiam tribum Manasse, transferret in Mediam. Socrates historia ecclesiastica libro 7. capite 10. Fertur, inquit, Alaricum proficiscentem Romam virum quendam religiosum, vita monachum, monuisse, ne de tantis malis gauderet, nec caedibus & sanguine delectaretur: cui ille respondit, Ego quidem mea sponte illuc non proficiscor, sed est qui me singulis diebus vrgeat torqueatque dicens, abi Roma vrbem deuasta, &c. Non igitur in gratia hominum cum verbo Dei pugnantia suscipienda sunt: Deus ex inimicis potest nobis amicos facere, Prou. 16. & vicis im ex amicis hostes.
units.tr: 2. We have an example of that saying of Proverbs 21: "Like streams of water, the heart of the king is in the hand of the Lord; he turns it wherever he wills." This sentence is to be understood not only of kings but also of private persons, whose hearts he also bends wherever he wills, so that they do what otherwise they would by no means have done. Cyrus would not have wished to be without the labour of the Jews, but God brings it about that he sets them free. We have other examples of this matter in this book. In this chapter there is the people whose spirit God is said to have stirred up. In chapter 5, Tithnai and his associates showed themselves humane towards the Jews and almost interceded for them with the king. In chapter 6, Darius sought out the decree of Cyrus and commanded his men not to hinder those who were building, etc. I will cite another example from Josephus, about Alexander the Great, who finally overthrew the Persian monarchy which this Cyrus had built up. He moved with an army against the Jews at Jerusalem, whom he was hostile to because they had not brought help to him when he besieged Tyre, and asked for it, on account of the benefits they had received from the Persian kings. Jaddus, the high priest, adorned with his robe, and the priests and likewise the elders, poured out to meet him, to beg for peace as suppliants. When Alexander saw the high priest, he got down from his horse and greeted him. When the commanders asked him why he humbled himself in this way, he answered that in Macedonia such a figure had appeared to him in a dream, and had bidden him make war on the Persians, and that he was helped by God, whose servant he was. And in the first book of Chronicles, chapter 5, God is also said to have stirred up the spirit of Pul, king of Assyria, and the spirit of Tiglath-pileser, king of Assyria, so that they carried the Reubenites, the Gadites and the half-tribe of Manasseh over into Media. Socrates, in his Ecclesiastical History, book 7, chapter 10, reports that when Alaric was setting out for Rome, a certain religious man, a monk by his way of life, warned him not to rejoice at such great evils, nor take delight in slaughter and blood. He answered: "I am not going there of my own accord, but there is someone who urges and harasses me every day, saying: go to Rome and lay the city waste." Therefore things that clash with the word of God are not to be undertaken for the sake of men's favour. God can make friends of our enemies, Proverbs 16, and conversely enemies of friends.

units.la: 3 Nisi spiritus sanctus nostras quoque mentes moueat, nihil recte & laude dignum faciemus. Natura enim nil recte cogitare, nedum facere possumus. Nisi Cyrus motus fuisset sancto spiritu, maiorem priuati sui commodi, quàm Israelitarum & gloriæ diuinæ rationem habuisset. Spiritus domini torporem nobis excutit.
units.tr: 3. Unless the Holy Spirit moves our minds also, we shall do nothing rightly or worthy of praise. For by nature we cannot think rightly, much less act rightly. Unless Cyrus had been moved by the Holy Spirit, he would have had more regard for his own private advantage than for the Israelites and the glory of God. The Spirit of the Lord shakes off our torpor.

units.la: 4 Ne diuturnis malis fracti, salutem desperemus. Israelitæ annis 70. deformem seruitutem passi sunt, ingentes dolores sustinuerunt, erexerunt tamen se spe liberationis, freti diuinis promissionibus. Idem faciant qui sub tyrannis degentes, multa mala propter puriorem doctrinam perferunt: cogitantes breue esse vitæ tempus. Deus ex omnibus malis publicis & priuatis, mox possetnos liberare, sed non esset è re nostra: nos itaq; totos Dei gubernationi commendemus, in morbis, p aupertate, & aliis grauibus tentationibus, maximè si caro fluctuare incipiat.
units.tr: 4. Let us not, broken by long-lasting evils, despair of salvation. The Israelites suffered a shameful servitude for seventy years and endured huge pains, yet they raised themselves up with the hope of deliverance, relying on divine promises. Let those who live under tyrants and suffer many evils for a purer doctrine do the same, reflecting that the time of life is short. God could at once free us from all public and private evils, but it would not be for our good; so let us commit ourselves wholly to God's governance, in sicknesses, in poverty, and in other grave temptations, especially if the flesh begins to waver.

units.la: 5 Quod Deus illas res, quas putamus nullo modo fieri posse, nullo negotio perficiat. Confitemur eum in capitibus fidei nostræ, omnipotentem esse. Quis fore putaret, vt vrbs Babylon euerteretur, quæ tam fuit munita, vt incolæ Cyrum in obsidione riderent? Quis putaret populum Dei reducendum? Probabile non erat, manu mittendos à Babylonijs, qui eorum opera vsi sunt, & magnam ex eis vtilitatem perceperunt: Deinde nemo erat qui vel posset vel vellet eos in libertatem asserere: ipsi non potuerunt aspirare ad libertatem, cum dispersi, pauci numero & inermes essent: neq; spes erat Medos & Persas, qui iure belli illis dominabantur, carere velle illis commodis, quæ ex ipsis percipere poterant. Deus autem effecit, vt euolutis fatalibus illis annis, Cyrus illos non modo libenter dimitteret, sed donis insuper ornaret, imò oneraret. Ne igitur rebus quantumuis afflictis & desperatis, animum abijciamus, sed cogitemus Deum facile posse nobis opitulari, intuentes in eius promissiones.
units.tr: 5 That God accomplishes with no effort those things which we think cannot be done in any way. We confess in the articles of our faith that He is almighty. Who would have thought that the city of Babylon would be overthrown, a city so well fortified that its inhabitants mocked Cyrus during the siege? Who would have supposed that the people of God would be brought back? It was not likely that the Babylonians would let them go free, since they had used their labour and derived much advantage from them. Moreover, there was no one who could or would set them at liberty. The exiles themselves could not aspire to freedom, being scattered, few in number and unarmed; nor was there any hope that the Medes and Persians, who ruled over them by right of war, would wish to give up the benefits they could draw from them. But God brought it about that, when those fated years had run their course, Cyrus not only let them go willingly but even loaded them with gifts, indeed burdened them. Therefore let us not give up in heart, however afflicted and hopeless our circumstances, but let us reflect that God can easily help us, looking to His promises.

units.la: HOMILIA III.
units.tr: HOMILY III.

units.la: Edictum Cyri.
units.tr: The Edict of Cyrus.

units.la: 1 Sic dixit Chores Rex Paras, omnia regna terra dedit mihi Iehouah Deus cœli: & ipse præcepit mihi vt ædificem ei domum in Ierusalaim, quæ est in Iehudah.
units.tr: 1 Thus says Cyrus, king of Persia: The LORD God of heaven has given me all the kingdoms of the earth, and he has commanded me to build him a house in Jerusalem, which is in Judah.

units.la: 3 Quis est inter vos de vniuerso populo eius?
units.tr: 3 Who is there among you of all his people?

units.la: fit Deus eius cum eo, & ascendat in Ierusalaim, quae est in Iehudah, atq; ædificet domum Iehouae Dei Israelis (ipse est Deus) quae est in Ierusalaim.
units.tr: May his God be with him, and let him go up to Jerusalem, which is in Judah, and build the house of the LORD, the God of Israel (he is God), which is in Jerusalem.

units.la: 4. Quisquis autem remanserit, ex omnibus locis in quibus peregrinatur, subleuabunt viri loci sui argento & auro, & substantia, & iumentis, cum oblatione spon tanea domui quae est in Ierusalaim.
units.tr: 4. And whoever remains, from all the places where he is a stranger, let the men of his place support him with silver and gold, with goods and with beasts, together with a freewill offering for the house which is in Jerusalem.

units.la: PRædictionibus sanctorum prophetarum, Apostolorum, & in primis seruatoris nostri IESV CHRISTI, euentus vel iam respondit, vel suo tempore respondebit, vtutres longe secus habere videantur. Hoc cum multis exemplis declarari possit, illo contenti erimus, quod hoc capite nobis à spiritu sancto proponitur. Iudaei abducti fuerunt in captiuitatem Babyloni-cam, ex qua Ieremias euolutis 70. annis liberandos & reducendos prædixit. Isaias liberatoris nomen expressit, statim igitur elapsis annis illis fatalibus (Cyri monarchiæ annus primus, fuit vltimus captiuitatis) Deus Cyrum impulit suo spiritu, vt voce preconum, & edictis propositis, per sua regna promulgaret, facultatem dare populo Dei redeundi in patriam. Edictu eius his ipsis verbis continetur, & postea repetitur capite 6.
units.tr: Although the events have either already answered, or will in their own time answer, the predictions of the holy prophets, the apostles, and above all of our Saviour Jesus Christ, so that they may seem to have turned out quite otherwise, this could be shown with many examples, but we shall be content with what the Holy Spirit sets before us in this chapter. The Jews were carried off into Babylonian captivity, from which Jeremiah foretold that they would be freed and brought back after seventy years had passed. Isaiah named the liberator. Therefore, as soon as those fated years had elapsed (the first year of Cyrus's monarchy was the last year of the captivity), God stirred Cyrus by his Spirit to publish, through the voice of heralds and by posted edicts throughout his realms, the permission given to God's people to return to their homeland. His edict is contained in these very words, and it is repeated later in chapter 6.

units.la: Habet autem tres præcipuas partes. 1. Est confessio Cyri de Deo Israelis. 2. Concedit populo, vt in patriam redeat. 3. Hortatur suos subiectos, vt Iudaeis pauperibus & infirmis auxilio sint, quo posint in patriam suam redire.
units.tr: It has three principal parts. (1) Cyrus's confession concerning the God of Israel. (2) He grants the people leave to return to their homeland. (3) He exhorts his subjects to help the poor and weak Jews, so that they may be able to return to their homeland.

units.la: Audiamus primo loco egregiam confessionem Cyri. Magnificè loquitur de Deo Israelis: Vocat eum Deum cœli, non quòd maiestas eius cœlis contineri possit, implet enim cœlum & terram sua gloria: sed quod præcipuè in cœlis suam potentiam nobis conspiciendam præbeat, mox dicit, ipse est Deus: scilicet verus & solus Deus, Isaiae 45. qui est in Hierusalem. Illam enim de legit in locum cultus sui, & per multa miracula ostendit se ibi esse præsentem. Confitetur se ab illo Deo, sua regna accepisse: non suis viribus, prudentiæ, consilijs tribuit, vt Senacherib & alij, sed soli Deo. Omnia regna. Est hyperbole vel synechdoche, pro multis & magnis, non specialiter omnibus: vel sensus est, quotquot posideo, Dei beneficio cofecut sum. Imperia enim Deus constituit, tuetur ac conseruat. Ipse constituit & deponit reges & principes. Paulus ad Romanos 13. potestatem à Deo ordinatam dicit, & qui potestati resistit, resistere ordinationi diui
units.tr: Let us hear first the noble confession of Cyrus. He speaks magnificently of the God of Israel. He calls him the God of heaven, not because his majesty can be contained in heaven, for he fills heaven and earth with his glory, but because he displays his power to us especially in the heavens. Then he says, "he is God," that is, the true and only God (Isaiah 45), "who is in Jerusalem." For he chose that place for his worship and showed by many miracles that he was present there. He confesses that he has received his kingdoms from that God. He does not attribute them to his own strength, prudence, or counsels, as Sennacherib and others did, but to God alone. "All the kingdoms": this is a hyperbole or synecdoche for many and great ones, not literally all; or the sense is, however many I possess, I have obtained by the benefit of God. For God establishes empires, protects and preserves them. He himself appoints and deposes kings and princes. Paul in Romans 13 says that power is ordained by God, and whoever resists the power resists the ordinance of God, and therefore will be punished. All histories testify that in every age seditious men have been given heavy punishments. Princes, moreover, ought to remember that they are the clients and ministers of God, and that they ought not to stretch out their hand over his jurisdiction. He adds that he has received a command from God to build him a temple in Jerusalem, that is, to help the efforts of his people in building the temple. Isaiah 60 prophesied that the nations would contribute their labour to the building of the Church.

units.la: Partes edi / fi. — Confessio Cyri. næ,& propterea pœnis affici. Seditiosos enim omnibus seculis pœnas graues dedisse,omnes historiæ testantur. Principes autem meminisse debent,se Dei esse clientes & ministros,nec debere manum suam extendere in eius iuris dictionem. Addit,se à Deo in mandatis accepisse,vt ipsi templum in Ierusalem ædificet,hoc est,vt populi sui conatus iuuet in ædificio templi. Isaias 6o. vaticinatus est,fore vt gentes suam operam ad ecclesiæ ædi ficationem collaturi sint.
units.tr: Whence, indeed, did Cyrus have this knowledge of God? From the revelation of the Holy Spirit, from the prophecy of Isaiah, and so on. God today also asks princes to build him a spiritual house, that is, they should take up the true care of the Church, that is, of his faithful, defend them, and see that they are rightly instructed. The Church is built in individual men and in many, when the ignorance of God, evil lusts, pride and injustice are driven out, and when his glory is planted. In some previous centuries, princes, led by a certain superstition, built many temples and monasteries magnificently and at great expense, which they commonly call houses of God, yet they held true doctrine in little regard, though it ought above all to have been their concern and their heart's desire. Although the greatest account must be taken of the spiritual temple, nevertheless those external temples must not be neglected on account of the pure religion that is exercised in them. In our own time there are perhaps not lacking those who would prefer to build brothels rather than the house of God, or the houses of the ministers of the Word.

units.la: Vnde vero habuit hanc Dei cognitionem Cyrus? Ex reuelatione spiritus sanḉti,& ex Isaiæ vaticinio,&c. Deus hodie quoque à principibus postulat,vt domum ei spiritualem construat hoc est,veram ecclesiæ,id est, fidelium suorum curam suscipiant,eos defendant,rectè erudiendos curent. Ædificatur ecclesia in singulis hominibus & pluribus, quando repellitur ignorantia Dei, prauæ libidines,superbia,iniustitia,& quando gloria eius plantatur. Superioribus aliquot seculis, principes superstitione quadam ducti,multa templa & monasteria(quæ vulgo domus Dei vocant)magnifice magnis sumptibus extruxerunt,interim veræ doctrinæ paruam habuerunt rationem,quæ in primis illis curæ & cordi esse debuit. Quanquam vero spiritualis templi maxima ratio habenda sit, tamen externa illa templa,propter puram religionem quæ in eis exercetur, non sunt negligenda. Non desunt fortassis nostra tempestate qui lupanaria mallent extruere,quàm domum Dei, aut domos ministrorum Verbi.
units.tr: Let private men too learn from the example of Cyrus to speak magnificently of God. Surely that most powerful king is not ashamed to proclaim the God of Israel and to invite others to worship him. David could never be satisfied, as the reading of the Psalms shows, in singing the praises of God. Today many are ashamed to speak of God in company, or to recite the Lord's Prayer at table with others listening. Yet they are not ashamed to empty great cups, or to injure the good name of others, and so on.

units.la: Discant priuati quoq; homines exemplo Cyri,magnificè de Deo loqui. Non pudet potentissimum illum regem, Deum Israelis prædicare, & alios inuitare ad ipsum colendum. Dauid nunquam sibi satisfacere potuit,vt ex Psalmorum lectione apparet, in decantandis Dei laudibus. Multos hodie pudet de Deo loqui in cœtibus hominum,aut ad mensam aliis audientibus recitare orationem dominicam. Interim non pudet eos ex siccare magna pocula: aliorum samam lædere,&c.
units.tr: As Cyrus ascribes his kingdoms to God alone, so we ought to ascribe our liberty, wealth, power, good health and other things to God, not to our own toil or industry, and we ought not to grow proud on account of the gifts received from God, but to devote them to the building up of his Church.

units.la: Vt Cyrus sua regna soli Deo accepta fert,ita nos libertatem, opes,potentiam,bonam valetudinem & alia, Deo,non nostro labori vel industriæ ascribere,nec insolescere debemus propter dona à Deo accepta, sed ad ædificationem ecclesiæ ipsius illa conferre.
units.tr: As Cyrus acknowledges that his kingdoms are received from God alone, so we ought to ascribe our liberty, wealth, power, good health and other blessings to God, not to our own labour or industry. We should not grow proud over the gifts we have received from God, but should devote them to building up his Church.

units.la: Secundo loco Cyrus liberum facit Iudæis,vt qui volunt domum redeant: imò iubet eos in patriam proficisci. Decem quoque tribubus Israelis, concessa fuit illa libertas, sed paucos ex illis
units.tr: In the second place, Cyrus grants the Jews freedom to return home if they wish; indeed he orders them to set out for their homeland. That same freedom was also granted to the ten tribes of Israel, but only a few of them returned. We shall hear about those in their place.

units.la: Cyrm Iudæis concedit vt in patriam redeant. illis redijscfuo loco audiemus. Illis qui sunt de populo Dei, rex fausta precatur:nō rebelles,pertinaces vocat, autalijs male distis illos grauat:vt hodie papistæ Euangelicos solent.Non di cit,liberabimur illis pestibus,abeant in malam rem :sed honori fico elogio eos ornat. Iubet eos domino templum ædificare. Magnum hoc fuit,quod omnibus citra exceptione dat facultatem redeundi in patriam.Potuisset enim aliquos ingeniosos artifices sibi retinere,vt moris est apud aliquot gentes, & in primis Turcas.Apud nos qui frugi famulos aut ancillas habet, vix & ne vix quidè eas à se dimittunt. Et si aliquid difficile nobisq; valde incomodum sit,tamen Deo mandante est faciendū. Ethnici sua mancipia,si rectè se gessissent,sæpenumero manumise- runt:nostro vero tempore,nemo seruitutem acrius defendit & retinet quàm monachi.Dabunt principes illi Deo graues pœnas,qui surdi sunt ad preces pioru subiectoru, neq; eos volunt liberare ex seruitute illa graui Babylonica,sed Pharaonis instar magis magisq; iugum eorū aggrauant.Cumq; sciant eos multis iniustis oneribus premi,tamē de subleuandis eis,nequaquā cogitant.Dabunt & illi pœnas,qui cùm possent & deberent Babylonem deserere,tamen propter commoda temporaria id facere detrectant.
units.tr: Cyrus grants the Jews that they may return to their homeland. To those who belong to the people of God, the king wishes well. He does not call them rebels or obstinate, nor burden them with insults, as the Papists are wont to do with the evangelicals today. He does not say, "May we be delivered from these pests, may they go to the devil," but adorns them with an honourable title. He orders them to build the temple for the Lord. This was a great thing, that he gave everyone without exception the opportunity to return to their homeland. For he could have kept back some skilled craftsmen for himself, as is the custom among several nations, and above all among the Turks. Among us, anyone who has a thrifty male or female servant can scarcely bear to let them go. And even if something is difficult and very inconvenient for us, it must still be done, since God commands it. The heathen have often freed their slaves if they had behaved well; but in our own time no one defends and keeps serfdom more fiercely than the monks. Those princes will pay heavy penalties to God who are deaf to the prayers of their pious subjects, and who do not want to free them from that heavy Babylonian servitude, but rather, like Pharaoh, make their yoke heavier and heavier. Although they know that these people are oppressed by many unjust burdens, they do not think at all of lightening them. Those too will pay the penalty who, although they could and ought to leave Babylon, refuse to do so for the sake of temporary advantages.

units.la: Tertio loco rex mandat prouincialibus, vt iuuent illos,qui cupiant redire in patriá,sed non possint per egestate,& alia impedimenta.Viri loci sui,hoc est,cuiusq; oppidi vel pagi. Quidā de Iudæis interpretantur,qui in Babylone remanserūt propter possessiones quas acquisierant,alij de gentilibus qui subleuare pauperes,aut infirmos Iudæos debebant suis opibus & iumen tis, asinis,Camelis& alijs,vt possent domū redire.De vtrisq; potest comodè exponi.Fuerunt qui ad extructione templi aut sacrificia,sua sponte & liberaliter contulerunt,hi præter illam obligationem iam factă,etiá tenebantur suis opib⁹ pauperes subleuare:non enim hoc eos excusabat,quòd iā ante aliquid dedidissent.
units.tr: In the third place, the king commands the provincial governors to help those who wish to return to their homeland but cannot, on account of poverty and other hindrances. "Men of their place" means the men of each town or district. Some interpret this of the Jews who remained in Babylon because of the possessions they had acquired; others of the Gentiles, who ought to relieve poor or sick Jews with their wealth and with beasts of burden, asses, camels and the like, so that they might be able to return home. Either interpretation can fairly be explained. There were some who, of their own accord and generously, gave towards the building of the temple or for the sacrifices; these people, besides that obligation already undertaken, were also bound to relieve the poor with their means. For it did not excuse them that they had already given something before.

units.la: Opulenti homines,hodie quoque iuuare pauperes debent. Deus enim ideo ipsis dat opes ingentes,vt in alios quoq; benefici sint,1.Timoth.6.Si verò videantur ad rem esse attentiores, vrgendi sunt à principibus , vt pauperum rationem habeant. Multo magis cauere principes debent, ne vsurarij , propolæ, monopolæ, & aliæ id genus pestes annonæ,plebi nefarijs suis artibus molesti sint. Nam si eam prorsus exhauriunt, non habent principes aliud quod expectent ,. quàm seditiones & turbas.
units.tr: Wealthy people today too ought to help the poor. For God therefore gives them great riches, so that they may also be beneficent to others (1 Tim. 6). But if they seem to be too attentive to their own affairs, they must be urged by the princes to take account of the poor. Princes ought to be even more careful that usurers, forestallers, monopolists and other pests of that kind, who harm the common people by their wicked arts and so raise the price of grain, do not do so. For if they drain the supply entirely, the princes have nothing left to look for but seditions and disturbances.

units.la: IN LIBRVM ESDRAE HOMILIA IIII.
units.tr: ON THE BOOK OF EZRA, HOMILY IV.

units.la: Obedientia Iudæorum & aliorum subiectorum Cyri.
units.tr: The obedience of the Jews and of the other subjects of Cyrus.

units.la: 5 Surrexerunt itaq; principes patrum Iehudah & Biniamin, ac Sacerdotes & Leuitæ, omnes quorum excitauerat Deus spiritum, vt ascenderent ad ædificandam domum Iehouæ quæ est in Ierusalaim.
units.tr: 5 Then the heads of the fathers of Judah and Benjamin rose up, and the priests and the Levites, all those whose spirit God had stirred up, to go up and build the house of Jehovah which is in Jerusalem.

units.la: 6 Omnes præterea qui erant in circuitu eorum, roborauerunt manus eorum vasis argenteis & aureis, substantia, & iumentis, & rebus pretiosis, præter omne quod sponte oblatum est.
units.tr: 6 Moreover, all who were round about them strengthened their hands with vessels of silver and gold, with goods, with beasts and with precious things, besides everything that was offered freely.

units.la: IN secunda parte huius capitis, commemoratur quomodo Iudæi & eorum vicini se gesserint, audito regio edicto. Iudæi iter ingressi sunt: quando, quinam & quare id fecerint, indicatur.
units.tr: In the second part of this chapter it is recorded how the Jews and their neighbours conducted themselves when they heard the royal edict. The Jews set out on the journey; when, who and why they did so is shown.

units.la: Mox a diuulgato edicto Cyri profectionem susceperunt, quantumuis laboriosam & periculosam, rem non distulerunt in aliud tempus.
units.tr: Immediately after the edict of Cyrus was published, they undertook the journey, however laborious and dangerous it was, and did not put the matter off to another time.

units.la: Qui nam? Omnibus quidem nullo excepto, permissum imo præceptum erat, vt in patriam redirent: sed nunc non omnes se ad iter accinxerunt, sed tantum capita patrum ex tribu Iuda & Beniamin. Deinde sacerdotes & Leuitæ. Hæ tribus in laceratione regni, domui Dauidis adhæserant, & multi ex illis cum Ioachim & Iechonia abducti erant, neq; illi omnes iter ingressi sunt: sed quorum spiritum Dominus excitauit, hoc est, quorum corda commouit, & mentes impulit. Seniores & duces hoc loco, & passim in scripturis appellantur capita. Deut. 1. dicit Moses se capita populo præfecisse, &c. propter multa quæ cum capite corporis humani, similia habent. Hac autem metaphora dignitas vel authoritas, munus vel officiu & necessitas magistratus ostenditur: item officium subditorum erga suum magistratum. Vt caput collocatum est in summo, super omnia membra, quæ illi subiecta sunt tanquam domino totius corporis, sic Deus magistratum suis subditis præfecit, vt sit dominus ipsorum. Sicut caput ratione regit totum corpus: ita Magistratus regere debet suos subditos. Caput neruos diffundit ad singula membra, quibus ea sibi retinet inter se connexa. Varro caput putat dictum quod inde initium capiant piant nerui, organa sensus & motus : sic magistratus sub-ditos in vnitate conferuare debet. Caput videt & audit pro toto corpore, & omnibus membris, sic à magistratu requi-ritur,vt videat ne refpublica detrimentum accipiat. Caput ca-pit cibum, qui diffunditur ad omnia membra, vt illo nutrian-tur: ita magistratus fouere debet corpus reipublicæ, eiusque commodis consulere. Si caput male habet, totum corpus lan-guet:capite sublato à corpore,perit illud:ita refpublica quæ ma giftratu caret, consistere non potest. ἀναρχία est pernities cu-iusque populi. Deinde quia scriptura principes capita vocat, subditi honore eos afficere debent: eosque defendere,vt caput obiectu brachiorum defendimus. Etsi verò magistratus suos næuos habeat: tamen cogitandum nos quoque nostris vitijs laborare.
units.tr: Who were they? Not all of them, without exception, were permitted, indeed commanded, to return to their homeland; but not all of them girded themselves for the journey, only the heads of the fathers of the tribes of Judah and Benjamin, then the priests and the Levites. These tribes had adhered to the house of David when the kingdom was torn apart, and many of them had been carried away with Joachim and Jechoniah; yet not all of them set out, but those whose spirit the Lord stirred up, that is, whose hearts he moved and whose minds he impelled. Elders and leaders are called "heads" in this place and throughout the Scriptures. In Deuteronomy 1 Moses says that he had set heads over the people, etc., on account of the many points in which they resemble the head of the human body. By this metaphor the dignity or authority, the office or duty and the necessity of the magistrate is shown, and likewise the duty of subjects towards their magistrate. As the head is placed on top, above all the members, which are subject to it as to the lord of the whole body, so God has set the magistrate over his subjects, to be their lord. As the head by reason rules the whole body, so the magistrate ought to rule his subjects. The head sends its nerves out to the individual members, by which it keeps them connected to one another; so the magistrate ought to preserve his subjects in unity. Varro thinks the word caput (head) is derived from the fact that the nerves, the organs of sense and motion, take their beginning from it; so the magistrate must keep his subjects together in unity. The head sees and hears for the whole body and all its members; so it is required of the magistrate that he see to it that the commonwealth suffer no harm. The head receives food, which is distributed to all the members so that they may be nourished by it; so the magistrate ought to cherish the body of the commonwealth and look to its advantage. If the head is ill, the whole body languishes; when the head is cut off from the body, the body perishes; so a commonwealth that lacks a magistrate cannot stand. Anarchia [ἀναρχία] is the ruin of every people. Further, because Scripture calls rulers "heads", subjects ought to honour them, and defend them as we defend the head by interposing our arms. And although magistrates may have their blemishes, we must nonetheless remember that we too labour under our own faults.

units.la: Quæris,Cur Deus alios non etiam commouerit?Nimirum vt cum pauci initio ascenderent, commeatum possent facilius habere. Deinde vt cognitio & gloria Dei,per illos qui inter gen tes permanserant in Babylone,latius propagaretur, per Danie-lem enim & alios, multos conuersos esse,certum est. Atque sic Deus captiuitatem illam, tum Iudæis,tum alijs in bonum con-uertit.
units.tr: You ask: why did God not stir up the others as well? Surely so that, since only a few set out at first, they might more easily obtain provisions for the journey. Next, so that the knowledge and glory of God might be spread more widely through those who had remained among the nations in Babylon; for it is certain that through Daniel and others many were converted. And so God turned that captivity to good, both for the Jews and for the others.

units.la: Hierosolymam profecti sunt, vt Domini templum extrue-ret. Multa potuissent illorum iter retardare. Potuissent dicere, pauci fumus, expectabimus donec certi aliquid habeamus de fratribus nostris, quid illi facturi sint: iter longum est & difficile, loca ad quæ tendimus sunt vasta & inculta, vrbes in ruinis iacent:barbari hostes incolunt terram,principum mentes faci-le mutantur,& alia id genus.At quia Deus corda eorum vera fi-de accenderat, committunt fe itineri, freti ipsius promissionibus. Quæ fit fidei vis ad Hebræos ii. cap.multis illustribus exemplis declaratur.Postea alij quoq; ascenderunt.
units.tr: They set out for Jerusalem so that they might build the temple of the Lord. Many things could have delayed their journey. They could have said: we are few; we will wait until we have certain news of our brethren, what they intend to do. The journey is long and hard, the places to which we are heading are waste and uncultivated, the cities lie in ruins, barbarian enemies inhabit the land, the minds of princes change easily, and other such things. But because God had kindled their hearts with true faith, they committed themselves to the journey, trusting in his promises. What the power of faith is, is declared by many illustrious examples in Hebrews chapter 11. Afterwards others also set out.

units.la: Vltimo hoc tempore, pauci viri politici & ecclesiastici,populum ex Babylonica captiuitate Antichristi eduxerunt, licet hoc initio nequaquam fieri posse crederetur.Deus enim plures excitauit,qui eis auxilio fuerunt.Si non statim multi seiungant nobis,non offendamur.Romam vulgo dicunt,non vno die con ditam esse. Quod autem absque Dei auxilio nil possimus, hæc phrafis ostendit,Deum excitaffe spiritum eorum,vt viam ingrederentur. 2.Corint.3. Non fumus idonei per nos ipsos cogitare aliquid boni. Deus suo spiritu nos corroborat,& impedimenta quæ obijciuntur viam salutis ingressis,remouet.
units.tr: In our own time, a few political and ecclesiastical men have led the people out of the Babylonian captivity of Antichrist, although at the beginning it was not believed that this could be done at all. For God stirred up more men who were helpers to them. If many do not immediately join us, let us not be offended. They commonly say that Rome was not founded in a single day. That we can do nothing without the help of God is shown by this expression, that God stirred up their spirit so that they would enter upon the way. 2 Corinthians 3: "We are not sufficient of ourselves to think anything as of ourselves." God strengthens us by his Spirit, and removes the obstacles that are thrown in the way of those who enter the way of salvation.

units.la: Si offeratur nobis occasio libertatis vel animi vel corporis, eam non repudiemus. D. Paulus 1. Corin. 7. Seruus vocatus es? ne sit tibi curæ, attamen si potes liber fieri, potius vtere. Ridentur Cappadoces qui cum Romani eos libertate donarent, propter multa in Rempublicam merita, maluerunt serui esse, negantes se viuere posse sine rege, teste Iustino lib. 38. Cicero secunda Philippica. Seruitus postremum est omnium malorum, nō modo bello, sed etiam morte repellendum. Hodie multi animi libertatem à Deo oblatam contumaciter reijciunt.
units.tr: If an opportunity of liberty, whether of mind or of body, is offered to us, let us not refuse it. The apostle Paul, 1 Corinthians 7: "Were you called as a servant? Do not be concerned about it; but if you can become free, rather use it." The Cappadocians are ridiculed, who, when the Romans gave them their freedom because of their many services to the commonwealth, preferred to remain slaves, saying that they could not live without a king; so Justin, book 38. Cicero, Second Philippic: slavery is the last of all evils, to be repelled not only by war but even by death. Today many stubbornly reject the liberty of the soul offered to them by God.

units.la: Principes, sacerdotes & Leuitæ, simul proficiscuntur. Vtile si hodie quoque sint concordes, & plebem suo exemplo ducant. Plurimum enim possunt exempla principum in vtramque partem.
units.tr: The princes, the priests and the Levites set out together. It would be useful if, today too, they were of one mind and led the common people by their example. For the examples of princes have great power for good or for ill.

units.la: Quia Gentiles vident Cyrum fauere Iudæis, qui ante eos oderant, nunc iuuant pro virili. Iam enim subiungitur quid gentes vicini Iudæorum fecerint, roborarunt manus Iudæorum, hoc est, certatim iuuerunt eos, vasis argenteis & aureis, suppellectile (רכוש rachath diuitias, suppellectilem vel substantiam interpretantur) iumetis vel pecoribus, donis, (migdonoth R. Solomon hoc loco dona exponit. Gen. 24. fructus terræ vel dulcia poma, authore Munstero) adhæc sua sponte non iusi, dederunt eis munera, scilicet ad alendos pauperes, & extructionem templi.
units.tr: Because the Gentiles saw Cyrus favouring the Jews, whom they had hated before, they now helped them to the best of their ability. For what follows tells what the neighbouring nations of the Jews did: they strengthened the hands of the Jews, that is, they vied with one another in helping them, with vessels of silver and gold, with household goods (רכוש [rachath], which they render as riches, or household goods or substance), with beasts or cattle, with gifts (migdonoth; R. Solomon explains this word here as gifts; see Genesis 24, and the fruits of the earth or sweet apples, according to Münster). Moreover, without being ordered to do so, they of their own accord gave them gifts, namely for the support of the poor and for the building of the temple.

units.la: Discunt subiecti exemplo Iudæorum & gentilium illorum, quo pacto se erga magistratum suum gerere debeant. Cum Cyrus Iudæis concedit, aut potius præcipit, vt reuertantur in patriam: mox se parant ad iter: Cum eorum vicinis gentibus man dat, vt auxilio sint Iudæis pauperibus vel infirmis, vt iter illud conficere posint, nihil non faciunt in eorum gratiam. Ita nos quoque magistratus nostri mandatis obediamus. Non illis tantum, quæ nostro commodo facere possumus, vt cum leges nobis præscribunt de frequentandis sacris concionibus, cum vetant militiam mercenariam, luxuriam, vsuras, & alia id genus: sed etiam in illis quæ difficilia sunt, & incommoda: vt si iubeant nos crebro tributa pendere. 1. Pet. 2. parere iubet seruos heris morosis. Illi gentiles plus conferunt Israelitis quàm rex petat: quot sunt hodie qui fraudant suum magistratum, quo ad publica debita, dicentes alioqui plus satis opulentos esse.
units.tr: Subjects learn from the example of those Jews and those Gentiles how they ought to conduct themselves towards their magistrate. When Cyrus granted, or rather commanded, the Jews to return to their homeland, they immediately prepared for the journey; when he ordered the neighbouring peoples to help the poor or weak Jews, so that they might be able to complete that journey, they did everything in their favour.
